2610.14281v1.title: TGSR: Text-Grounded Diffusion for Faithful Image Super-Resolution
2610.14281v1.authors: Zhiming Hu, Ran Zhang, Angela Ye, Raghav Goyal, Faraz Ali, Tristan Ty Aumentado-Armstrong, Samrudhdhi B. Rangrej, Konstantinos G. Derpanis, Iqbal Mohomed, Alex Levinshtein
2610.14281v1.ori_summary: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in image super-resolution (SR) by leveraging strong generative priors to enhance perceptual quality. However, for textual content, these priors often produce text hallucinations: non-existent or distorted text, which alter scene semantics and compromise model reliability. While recent methods focus on enhancing text generation, they do so indiscriminately, leaving hallucinations fundamentally unresolved. We argue the core problem is a lack of selective control. Therefore, we reformulate text SR as a selective generation problem: text is resolved only when reliable generation is expected, while other scene content is fully super-resolved. We introduce TGSR (Text-Grounded Super-Resolution), a test-time framework that progressively identifies and suppresses likely hallucinated text regions during generation. To enable this, we train dedicated detectors on a large-scale dataset curated from diverse diffusion-based SR outputs. TGSR consistently improves text fidelity across multiple backbones, increasing recognition precision by up to 17.68 points without degrading perceptual quality, underscoring the value of selective control in generative SR.
2610.14281v1.reasoning: Purely vision/image super-resolution paper with no relevance to ranking or auction mechanisms.

2610.14269v1.title: RoboFake: Are Deepfake Detectors Ready for Humanoid Face Robots?
2610.14269v1.ori_summary: Humanoid face robots can now move their lips in sync with speech and show detailed facial expressions. Give such a robot the face of a real person and drive it with generated speech, and you get a face forgery that happens in front of the camera: the camera records a real object, and no pixel is edited. We call this a RoboFake. In this paper we ask what current deepfake detectors do when they see a robot face. We test six public detectors trained on FaceForensics++ on video of a physical lip-syncing face robot, on a synthesized video of the same robot, and on rendered robot faces. All thresholds are fixed on FaceForensics++, and every result is compared with real human faces that went through the same processing as the robot videos. At a threshold that flags 5% of real faces, three detectors flag almost every physical robot frame, while two flag fewer than 7%. A matched human control and masking show that the response comes from the face, not from the processing or the background. However, it does not track synthesis: with only the face visible, three of the six detectors give the physical robot a higher fake score than its synthesized video. The response is also fragile, and light JPEG compression is enough to push most robot frames below the threshold for some detectors. Our results suggest that current detectors flag today's robots because their faces do not look human, not because they recognize a forgery. We release our evaluation protocol and code, and state three testable hypotheses about realistic, interactive RoboFakes.
2610.14269v1.reasoning: Deepfake detection for humanoid robots; unrelated to ranking, auctions, or e-commerce.

2610.14254v1.title: Image Diffusion Models Are Good 3D Human Motion Generators
2610.14254v1.authors: Siyuan Yang, Chong Wang, Hao Cheng, Jun Liu, Bihan Wen, Alex Kot, Hedvig Kjellstrom
2610.14254v1.ori_summary: Text-to-motion generation typically relies on dataset-specific skeletal representations, with models trained separately for benchmarks with different joint layouts. We investigate whether image diffusion architectures can model 3D human motion through a common image-compatible representation that accommodates heterogeneous skeletal layouts while preserving motion-specific kinematic structure. To this end, we organize root-centered joint trajectories into topology-informed joint--time images and model global root dynamics through a complementary latent stream. A motion autoencoder conditions local-motion decoding on the root latent, while a text-conditioned Scalable Interpolant Transformer (SiT) jointly generates both latent streams, with supervision on decoded 3D joint positions further constraining generation in motion space. In addition to dataset-specific models, we train a single motion autoencoder on HumanML3D and KIT-ML, followed by a single text-conditioned SiT shared across both datasets, preserving their respective skeletal definitions without skeleton retargeting to a common joint layout. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML show that our dataset-specific models achieve state-of-the-art performance, while shared training yields further gains on both benchmarks, demonstrating the benefits of shared modeling across heterogeneous skeletal layouts.
2610.14254v1.reasoning: Purely 3D human motion generation, unrelated to ranking or mechanisms.

2610.14253v1.title: SliderEdit++: Improved Slider Trajectories in Instruction-Based Image Editing
2610.14253v1.authors: Arman Zarei, Sayan Nag, Bryan Wang, Franck Dernoncourt, Varun Manjunatha, Nedim Lipka, Soheil Feizi, Samyadeep Basu
2610.14253v1.ori_summary: Slider-based control aims to give users continuous, fine-grained control over the intensity of individual edits in instruction-based image editing. However, existing approaches fail to deliver reliable continuous controllability: traversing a slider can produce abrupt visual jumps and non-monotonic changes, while jointly controlled sliders can interfere with one another. To systematically study these limitations, we introduce SlideBench, a comprehensive benchmark for continuous image editing spanning diverse editing categories and equipped with a unified suite of metrics quantifying monotonic progression, perceptual continuity, and inter-slider disentanglement. Building on these observations, we propose SliderEdit++, which explicitly regularizes the intermediate editing trajectory rather than supervising only its endpoints. Our method combines velocity- and semantic-space trajectory regularization with spectral control to encourage smooth, predictable slider traversal, together with a disentanglement objective that reduces interference between independently controlled edits. On SlideBench, SliderEdit++ achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving the overall score by 18.5% relative to the strongest baseline. At the same time, using a few-step editing backbone makes our method approximately 3x to 20x faster than existing slider-based approaches, enabling substantially more responsive interactive editing.
2610.14253v1.reasoning: Purely about image editing, unrelated to ranking or auction mechanisms.

2610.14207v1.title: Token-Budgeted Candidate Retrieval for 3D Scene-Grounded VLMs: Category Names vs. Pairwise Geometry
2610.14207v1.authors: Michał Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak
2610.14207v1.ori_summary: Under a fixed context budget, which objects and relations should a 3D scene-grounded VLM see first? On ScanNet indoor referring benchmarks (Dai et al., 2017), matching the query to object category names outperforms pairwise geometry scoring at every reported K. The gaps are largest at high recall. Analytic pairwise cues beat per-object cue scoring and query-agnostic kNN graphs, including on paraphrases. MiniLM and BGE-small still score higher on those splits. We evaluate token-budgeted candidate retrieval with axis-aligned boxes, a token-ratio metric, training-free baselines, two small encoders that match q to each object's category name, and QCRR (Query-Conditioned Relation Retrieval), a deterministic pairwise-geometry scorer. Across ScanRefer gt_val plus a custom 20% scan-id split of Nr3D and Sr3D (35,504 queries; not official ReferIt3D val), additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 on ScanRefer against QCRR's 0.626; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911 to 0.913 on ScanRefer and 0.941 to 0.947 on Nr3D. A corrected 3DGraphLLM harness (native Acc@0.25 0.67 on the full graph, n=300 ScanRefer queries) shows that context selection changes downstream accuracy under a matched object budget (Random 0.44, QCRR 0.56, MiniLM 0.67, oracle 0.70). Semantic retrieval beats hand-designed geometry on that harness. We will release the protocol, retriever implementations, and per-query outputs so new selectors can be swapped in without rewriting the analysis.
2610.14207v1.reasoning: 3D scene-grounded VLM retrieval, unrelated to ranking/auction mechanisms.

2610.14589v1.title: Attribute-Centric Vision-Language Alignment for Fine-Grained Gait Understanding
2610.14589v1.authors: Saihui Hou, Chenye Wang, Wenpeng Lang, Qiannan Guo, Zhengxiang Lan, Chao Fan, Shiqi Yu, Yongzhen Huang
2610.14589v1.ori_summary: Walking sequences reveal human-interpretable attributes related to body structure, posture, and motion. Gait attribute recognition provides a concrete route to fine-grained gait understanding by predicting these attributes. However, existing benchmarks provide limited fine-grained annotations, while classifier-based gait attribute recognition methods typically represent candidate classes through learned output weights rather than directly matching visual evidence with textual class representations. To address the annotation gap, we present RA-GAR, a large-scale, richly annotated multimodal benchmark for gait attribute recognition, containing 1,001 subjects, 242,729 walking sequences, and annotations for 15 static and motion gait attributes. We further propose Gait-VL, an attribute-centric vision-language alignment framework that recognizes gait attributes by matching attribute-specific multi-frame visual evidence with textual class prototypes. On the visual side, attribute-specific learnable queries aggregate RGB features across spatial locations and frames into per-attribute visual embeddings. On the language side, diverse descriptions expanded by a large language model are combined with context about relevant body regions to construct textual class prototypes. Beyond attribute recognition, we evaluate the transferability of the attribute-pretrained visual encoder by using it to replace generic upstream large vision models in identityoriented gait recognition pipelines; attribute pre-training uses no identity classification or metric-learning objectives. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art attribute recognition performance on RA-GAR and consistent improvements in downstream identity recognition across multiple pipelines and benchmarks, supporting the effectiveness and transferability of attribute-centric gait representation learning.
2610.14589v1.reasoning: Gait recognition from vision-language models is a biometric/vision topic unrelated to ranking or auction mechanisms.

2610.14512v1.title: Spatiotemporal Recognition of Abdominal Wall Layers During Optical Trocar Entry
2610.14512v1.authors: Shreeram Athreya, Andrew Melehy, Carter Prentice, Michael Robinson, Corey Arnold, James Wu, William Speier
2610.14512v1.ori_summary: Objective. To evaluate whether spatial context and temporal modeling improve tissue recognition during optical trocar entry, where multiple abdominal-wall tissues may be visible simultaneously. Methods. We retrospectively analyzed 71 recordings with 1,516 annotated keyframes and 29,151 clinician-annotated sectors. Each frame was divided into 28 polar-grid sectors assigned to nine tissue classes. Color, neighboring-sector, and positional features were used by a gradient-boosted emission classifier. The full pipeline added learned temporal smoothing, spatial regularization, an anatomically ordered hidden Markov model, and posterior blending. Five-fold cross-validation was grouped by recording, with cross-fitting to prevent within-recording leakage. Primary evaluation used clinician-derived targets; ablations assessed classification, probability quality, spatial consistency, and peritoneum-or-deeper onset timing. Results. The complete pipeline achieved accuracy 0.646, macro-F1 0.507, and macro-AUROC 0.882, versus 0.600, 0.440, and 0.861 for emissions alone. Macro-F1 improved by 0.066 across all five folds. Label changes decreased from 66.2 to 19.5 per sector-minute, and median onset error decreased from 15.58 to 2.45 seconds. Frames with a tissue-depth-code span of at least three decreased from 53% to 26%, versus 22% for clinician annotations. Performance remained limited for preperitoneal fat and bowel, and the full model retained a 44% premature-onset proportion. Conclusions. Combining appearance, spatial context, and temporal constraints improved retrospective tissue recognition and onset localization. Tissue-specific limitations, residual timing errors, and reliance on future observations warrant external validation and prospective evaluation of causal models before clinical use.
2610.14512v1.reasoning: Domain-specific medical/surgical application unrelated to ranking or mechanism design.

2610.14403v1.title: VisualCoding: Learning Executable Skills for Reliable Visual Reasoning
2610.14403v1.authors: Liu Jiaqi, Jin Ruinan, Li Xiaoxiao
2610.14403v1.ori_summary: Learning reusable skills can improve visual reasoning agents, yet applying a skill still requires the agent to implement or invoke a procedure and produce the final answer. Errors and hallucinations at these steps can prevent acquired experience from translating into reliable single-run performance. We propose VisualCoding, which combines execution-guided acquisition of reusable visual programs with direct adoption of their answers on applicable inputs. Execution-Guided Program Acquisition composes visual primitives and additional code into family-level solvers, then iteratively tests and revises them on labeled training instances. Scope-Aware Direct Execution runs a retained solver and returns its valid in-scope answer. We evaluate VisualCoding on four models across four benchmarks spanning 69 task families. VisualCoding exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in mean accuracy by 4.45 percentage points with Gemini-3.1-Pro and by 14.78 points when reusing the frozen Pro-acquired artifacts with Flash-Lite. Ablations support execution-guided acquisition and show that direct execution outperforms textual or callable reuse of the same programs. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaq-liu/VisualCoding.

2610.14630v1.title: DuSRFlow: Dual-Lens Super-Resolution via Parallax-Aware Flow Estimation and Complementary Reference Warping
2610.14630v1.authors: Fangpu Zhang, Huanjing Yue, Zifan Cui, Shaoxiong Tu, Qirui Yang, Jingyu Yang
2610.14630v1.ori_summary: Dual-lens super-resolution (DuSR) aims to enhance a wide-angle low-resolution (LR) image by exploiting a telephoto reference (Ref) image. A central challenge in DuSR is reliable reference utilization under large parallax, occlusion, and cross-camera imaging discrepancies. Existing methods often employ off-the-shelf monocular optical flow models to provide geometric priors. However, their assumptions of photometric consistency and smooth motion are violated in dual-lens scenarios, leading to unreliable alignment and degraded reference-based reconstruction. To address these issues, we propose DuSRFlow, a dual-lens super-resolution framework that improves reference utilization from both correspondence learning and reference aggregation. First, we introduce DuFlowNet, a dedicated dual-lens flow estimator for robust cross-view alignment. To train DuFlowNet without ground-truth flow annotations, we develop a real--synthetic data fusion strategy that composites synthetic foreground objects onto real dual-lens image pairs, generating controllable large-parallax samples while preserving realistic cross-camera imaging characteristics. Second, we observe that reference reliability is highly spatially uneven in DuSR, where unreliable local reference responses may suppress the utilization of reliable cues. We therefore propose a Complementary Reference Warping strategy that coordinates patch-based warping and kernel-free-guided deformable warping according to local reference reliability, producing a more reliable reference representation before LR--Ref fusion. In addition, we construct DuSR-RealV2, a challenging real-world benchmark with complex depth variations, large parallax, and occlusion. Extensive experiments on multiple DuSR benchmarks demonstrate that DuSRFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance in reconstruction quality, perceptual quality, and cross-dataset generalization.

2610.14091v1.title: Pristine Models
2610.14091v1.authors: Anirudh Sundara Rajan, Krishna Kumar Singh, Richard Zhang, Yong Jae Lee
2610.14091v1.ori_summary: Training on broad, unfiltered data enables high-quality image generation, but can also teach models concepts that should not be generated; restricting the training data ensures safety, but reduces quality because examples containing unsafe concepts also provide useful knowledge that is not itself unsafe. Existing approaches largely address this trade-off post hoc through concept unlearning, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting as the number of concepts to remove grows. We instead ask whether unsafe concept knowledge can be compartmentalized during pretraining so that access to it can be disabled at inference. We introduce Pristine Models, a novel text-to-image generation architecture with an attention mechanism that encourages the separation of safe and unsafe knowledge into independently parameterized branches. The branch-specific parameters are learned during training, while the unsafe branch can be detached at inference. On ImageNet, Pristine Models enable safer generation while retaining much of the utility of full-data pretraining, achieving higher image quality and better text alignment than training only on safe data or applying post-hoc concept removal. We further scale our approach to CC12M, demonstrating that it remains effective in a substantially larger and more diverse open-world pretraining setting.

2610.14445v1.title: FreeCHROMA: Generative Chroma Keying from Unaligned Background References
2610.14445v1.authors: Jiayi Wu, Tianfu Wang, Rui Zhao, Florian Schiffers, Zhimin Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yezhou Yang, Christopher Metzler, Yiannis Aloimonos
2610.14445v1.ori_summary: In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre-aligned backgrounds, focus on background-conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter-efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground-background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo-paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground-background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end-to-end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.

2610.14397v1.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
2610.14397v1.authors: Andrew Perrault, Anmol Takiar, Dominik Wienecki, Arnab Nandi
2610.14397v1.ori_summary: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. 2610.14598v1.title: Bidirectional Adaptive Transformers for Multimodal Anomaly Detection
2610.14598v1.authors: Yuxin Jiang, Yunkang Cao, Weiming Shen

2610.14517v1.title: We Have Been Interpreting Diffusion Transformer Backbone Behaviors Wrong
2610.14517v1.authors: Benyuan Meng, Longtao Huang, Yang Liu, Liang Lin
2610.14517v1.ori_summary: During a network forward call, diffusion backbones naturally produce many intermediate activations. If we evaluate each activation against an identical downstream benchmarking protocol, we can plot an inverted-U-shaped curve as the depth profile: the activation's performance goes up first and then down as we go into deeper layers. This is common knowledge in the diffusion model community, which inspires many applications including the widely-adopted REPA. However, the common interpretation of this depth profile may be inaccurate and incomplete: (i) The cause of this curve has long been treated as signal granularity changing from coarse to fine, but there has been little evidence in DiT backbones. (ii) The community has been mainly studying this phenomenon in a static way, without investigating how it changes across different training setups. In this work, we show a different mechanism picture for the profile, where the prediction target (e.g., $ε$, $u$, $x_0$) sits at the center. The semantically meaningful signal is only an intermediate by-product for predicting the target, while the prediction target is the real goal for the backbone. Furthermore, the choice of prediction targets as part of the training setup can predictably affect the curve's shape. With this updated interpretation, many applications of this depth profile can be better grounded and predicted. As an example, we show how to predict the near-optimal placement of REPA based on the prediction target of the training setup. The code is at https://github.com/Darkbblue/dit-compare.

2610.14332v1.title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling
2610.14332v1.authors: George Matthew, Guoqiang Zhang, Kenta Niwa
2610.14332v1.ori_summary: Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while an intermediate backbone evaluation provides new trace information to predict the remaining residual; this evaluation is reused by the following step. 2610.14325v1.title: Manifold Navigation Learning Using Recurrent Networks: Efficient Training Techniques
2610.14325v1.authors: Sarah Harkins Dayton, Sathya Rengaswami, Vasileios Maroulas, David L. Boothe, Ioannis D. Schizas
2610.14325v1.ori_summary: Position tracking is a well-studied problem in Euclidean navigation, yet comparatively little attention has been given to navigation on general manifolds, where motion is governed by the underlying geometry of the space. 2610.14293v1.title: GeoFix: Geometry Fixing for 4D Consistent Generation
2610.14293v1.authors: Yeobin Hong, Hyojun Go, Dohun Lee, Jeongjae Lee, Sunghwan Hong, Federico Tombari, Zhaochong An, Jong Chul Ye, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer

2610.14158v1.title: Video-Arena: A Scalable Agentic Video Benchmark for Spatiotemporal Capability
2610.14158v1.authors: Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yue Su, Xiangnan Wu, Zirong Chen, Run Luo, Tao Tan, Yinhe Zheng, Yiming Li

2610.14553v1.title: Adversarial Gradient Forcing for Robust Few-Step Autoregressive Video Generation
2610.14553v1.authors: Chenxi Xia, Yixuan Xu, Shan Liu, Jiapeng Wang, Maohua Li, Hanlin Tang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Weiyi Lu, Xinggao Liu
2610.14553v1.ori_summary: Autoregressive video generation models generate videos sequentially, with each new block conditioned on previously generated blocks. 2610.14609v1.title: EviScene: Beyond "Is It AI?" for Agentic Image Factuality Assessment
2610.14609v1.authors: ZiAn Wang, Ruiqi Liu, Zhengbo Zhang, Yi Han, Jialiang Shen, Ruoxin Chen, Manni Cui, Ximo Zhu, Jin Jiang, Mingzhe Liu, Linhao Wang, Wenhao Wang, Shu Wu

2610.14624v1.title: EarthAlign: Learning Language-Aligned Representations of Earth System Data

2610.14261v1.title: BigCell: Generating Gigapixel Whole-Slide Images
2610.14261v1.authors: Srikar Yellapragada, Alexandros Graikos, Zilinghan Li, Kostas Triaridis, Tarak Nath Nandi, Ji Dong K Bai, Beatrice Knudsen, Tahsin Kurc, Prateek Prasanna, Rajarsi R. Gupta, Ravi K Madduri, Joel Saltz, Dimitris Samaras

2610.14228v1.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
2610.14228v1.authors: Seungjun Yu, Hojun Choi, Seojeong Park, Jaeyo Shin, Hyunjung Shim
2610.14228v1.ori_summary: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. 2610.14153v1.authors: Jingyu Liu, Hao Jiang, Yikang Ding, Huafeng Shi, Xu Yang, Xiaoqiang Liu, Guoxin Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai

2610.14726v1.title: LightVAE: Towards Compact and Efficient Video Autoencoders
2610.14726v1.authors: Shiqiao Gu, Yang Yong, Fengjun Zhong, Ruihao Gong, Chengtao Lv, Xiangyu Fan, Lei Yang, Xianglong Liu

2610.15343v1.title: Across Viewpoints and Time: Trajectory-Generalizable Physical Attacks on World Models and Video Understanding Models
2610.15343v1.authors: Song Xia, Meiwen Ding, Chenqi Kong, Wenhan Yang, Xudong Jiang
2610.15343v1.ori_summary: World models and video understanding models are increasingly deployed in dynamic visual environments, yet their robustness to physical adversarial threats remains largely underexplored. We study whether a single physical adversarial texture can mislead the victim model across different real-world scenarios where observing viewpoints vary along uncontrolled object--camera trajectories. We identify that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories induce poorly aligned gradients for optimizing the adversarial texture. To address that, we propose the Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (TARA), which incorporates trajectory-aware optimization to capture the evolving geometric variations of a printed texture under real-world scenarios. To improve cross-instance optimization compatibility, TARA incorporates trajectory-aware contrastive alignment to encourage attacked representations from diverse video--trajectory instances to approach a shared adversarial region and then performs trajectory-aware task refinement to translate the aligned representation into task-level prediction errors. For reproducible evaluation, we develop a geometry-grounded tracking pipeline that provides physically plausible adversarial regions with temporally consistent trajectories on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Something-Something V2. We further collect real-world print-and-recapture videos to validate attack effectiveness under physical deployment conditions. Together, the annotated benchmarks and real-world captured data form a reproducible testbed for future evaluation. Notably, our results reveal that a single printable adversarial texture can persistently disrupt world models and video understanding models under physical conditions, highlighting the fundamental security challenge.

2610.15054v1.title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
2610.15054v1.authors: James P. Wolfe, Joshua B. Plotkin
2610.15054v1.ori_summary: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.
2610.15054v1.reasoning: Purely theoretical multi-agent game learning, no ranking or mechanism design application.

2610.15520v1.title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
2610.15520v1.authors: Trung Thanh Nguyen, Khaled Elbassioni, Jörg Rothe
2610.15520v1.ori_summary: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.

2610.16770v1.title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
2610.16770v1.ori_summary: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.

2610.16684v1.title: The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
2610.16684v1.authors: Petra Berenbrink, Thorsten Götte, Martin Hoefer, Tim Koglin
2610.16684v1.ori_summary: We study the \emph{voter model with opinion graph}, a generalization of the standard (pull) voter model that adds a notion of bounded confidence. In this process, we consider a finite set $A$ of $n$ agents. Each agent $u \in A$ has an opinion $x_u \in O$, where we model opinions as vertices in an undirected opinion graph $G = (O,E)$ with $|O|=q$. In each step, an agent $u$ interacts with another agent $v \in A$. In contrast to classical voting, $u$ adopts the opinion $x_v$ if and only if $x_v$ and $x_u$ are neighbors in $G$. The process is stable once all remaining opinions are an independent set in $G$. We analyze two variants of the process: the ordinary EdgeVOG process, which samples a pair of interacting agents uniformly at random from all possible pairs, and the productive EdgeVOG process, which samples only pairs with neighboring opinions in $G$. We show the following: - For every opinion graph and every initial configuration, ordinary EdgeVOG stabilizes within $O(n^2\log n)$ steps in expectation and with high probability. The expectation bound is asymptotically tight. For the productive EdgeVOG process, the expected stabilization time is exactly the initial number of compatible agent pairs, while $O(n^2\log n)$ steps suffice with high probability. - An opinion $i$ with initial support $s_i$ survives with probability at least $p_i:=s_i/(s_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}s_j)$. Further, let $μ= \sum_{i \in O} p_i$, then we show the probability that less than $(1-δ)μ$ opinions survive is at most $\exp(-δ^2μ/(2(Δ^2+1)))$ for every $0\leqδ\leq1$. -If $G$ has maximum degree $Δ$ and every opinion initially has support at most $\hat{s}$, then no opinion ever acquires more than $\tilde{O}(\min\{n,Δ^6\hat{s}\})$ agents with high probability. This yields near-linear stabilization bounds for productive EdgeVOG for a large class of configurations.

2610.17416v1.title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
2610.17416v1.ori_summary: I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand. Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness. Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

2610.14994v1.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Division via Subsidies
2610.14994v1.ori_summary: We study the relationship between fair division with $\textit{subsidies}$ and $\textit{best-of-both-worlds}$ (BoBW) fairness for indivisible items. The proof uses linear programming duality. As applications, the reduction gives alternative proofs of BoBW existence results for additive goods, chores, and mixtures of goods and chores. The converse of our general reduction holds for two agents but fails for three: We provide a four-good counterexample with monotone submodular valuations where an ex-ante envy-free and ex-post EF1 lottery exists, but no allocation is simultaneously EF1 and envy-freeable. 2610.14329v1.title: Assortment Optimization under the Mallows Model: Independent-Utility Choice Equivalence and Its Algorithmic Implications
2610.14329v1.ori_summary: The Mallows model is a well-established construct in preference modeling, describing random rankings through their Kendall-Tau distance from a reference permutation. Its compact parameterization and interpretable treatment of preference uncertainty have made it influential across statistics, machine learning, probability, and revenue management. In the latter domain, recent literature has studied the embedding of Mallows-driven choice into assortment optimization. Early approximation schemes in this context require stylized structural simplifications or restrictive parametric assumptions. In the absence of these levers, a highly involved quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme has subsequently been proposed, leaving wide open the question of whether near-optimal assortments can be computed in true polynomial time. The main contribution of this focused technical paper resides in closing these gaps by uncovering a striking independent-utility structure within Mallows choices, and turning this representation into a polynomial-time approximation scheme. Our central structural characterization explicitly constructs a single collection of mutually independent utilities, reproducing Mallows choice probabilities simultaneously for all offered sets. This exact choice equivalence connects pending Mallows-related challenges to the recent approximation framework of Bowers et al. (FOCS 2025) for assortment optimization under independent random utilities. We make this connection algorithmically feasible through a finite-support reduction that produces distributions of polynomial size while controlling revenue loss uniformly over all assortments. Fused together, these ingredients lead to an $O(n^{\tilde{O}(1/ε^2)})$-time approximation scheme for assortment optimization under the Mallows model, while allowing arbitrary product prices, concentration parameters, and modal rankings.

2610.14363v1.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
2610.14363v1.ori_summary: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of subpopulations (formally, of functions on the inputs, called auditors) if, for every subpopulation in the class and every value the predictor outputs, the average outcome among the members of that subpopulation who receive that value is close to the value itself. For finite classes, about $\varepsilon^{-3}$ samples are necessary and sufficient to learn a predictor with multicalibration error $\varepsilon$, but the algorithms that attain this rate enumerate the class, which is impossible for the large classes of interest. We ask how many samples suffice when the learner accesses the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the class. Its dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal for all learners. When $d$ is at least about $1/\varepsilon$, every learner that can only access the class through polynomially many ERM calls needs $\tildeΩ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples. Learners with unlimited computation need only $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}+d\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples, so the extra factor $1/\varepsilon$ on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. For swap multicalibration, which allows a different function from the class for each predicted value, $\tildeΘ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient. For estimating the error of a given predictor, the ordinary notion is the harder one: the swap error can be estimated with an ERM oracle, whereas the ordinary error is NP-hard to approximate even for classes with linear-time ERM. Consequently, there are classes for which it is computationally easier to learn a multicalibrated predictor than to compute the multicalibration error of a given predictor.

2610.15916v1.title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
2610.15916v1.ori_summary: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $Ω((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

2610.15932v1.title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
2610.15932v1.authors: Haichuan Wang, Anagha Satish, Jiale Zheng, Saisneha Ghatti, Lingkai Kong, Kai Wang, Milind Tambe

2610.17744v1.title: A Matroid Generalization of Weighted Popular Matching: Characterization and Algorithm

2610.15480v1.title: Lasso Games

2610.17980v1.title: Exact power indices for plurality-voting ensembles
2610.17980v1.authors: Ilie Sarpe, Theofanis Georgakopoulos, Aristides Gionis

2610.16943v1.title: Online Fair Division with Upgrade Recourse
2610.16943v1.ori_summary: We study the online fair division of indivisible goods. 2610.15476v1.title: Representation Theorems for Actual Powers over Two-Agent General Concurrent Game Frames
2610.15476v1.authors: Zixuan Chen, Fengkui Ju, Thomas Ågotnes
2610.15476v1.ori_summary: One of the most well-known connections between logic and games is Pauly's representation theorem: the induced powers of individuals and coalitions in concurrent game frames correspond, in a precise sense, to a certain class of neighborhood frames. The precise sense here is what is called alpha effectivity (or alpha power): the power of a coalition is characterized by the sets of states in which it can ensure that the outcome lies by taking some joint action. This definition is inherently monotonic, and, as pointed out by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019), that fact can obscure relevant information about the power structure in the game: we do not know whether two sets that a coalition has the power to enforce correspond to the same joint action or to different joint actions. It has recently been argued by Li and Ju (2025, 2026) that standard concurrent game frames rely on three assumptions that may, in some cases, be too strong: seriality, independence of agents, and determinism. This yields a total of eight different classes of general concurrent game frames. In this paper, assuming two agents, we prove that, in terms of actual powers, the eight classes of general concurrent game frames are represented by eight corresponding classes of neighborhood frames. This generalizes a result by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019).

2610.17443v1.ori_summary: We investigate the growth trajectory of online platforms operating as market makers in two-sided matching markets. Embedded in this growth process are intertemporal participation constraints that the platform must satisfy to attract and retain forward-looking servers. To explicitly account for the stochastic dynamics of a platform's gradual growth, we model the system as a Markov process. The platform admits servers at the maximum feasible rate until it reaches an endogenous target size, which can be smaller than the static market-clearing optimum. In the baseline model, seniority-based compensation acts as an operational substitute for financially subsidized growth: instead of using upfront subsidies to induce early server participation, the platform uses future cash flows to reward early servers for joining when demand is limited and for helping the platform reach later, higher-demand states.

2610.15008v1.ori_summary: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.

2610.14473v1.title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
2610.14473v1.authors: Lilian Sun, Henry Huang, Fucheng Warren Zhu, Giannis Daras, Constantinos Daskalakis
2610.14473v1.ori_summary: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen. Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.

2610.15516v1.title: Robust Proportionality Axioms for Additive Utilities
2610.15516v1.ori_summary: We study the model of participatory budgeting, in which a subset of candidates is selected subject to a budget constraint. Voters express their preferences by assigning a numerical utility to each candidate. Our focus is on formal analysis of proportionality, a central notion of fairness in multi-winner elections. Intuitively, proportionality means that each group of voters should influence the election outcome roughly in proportion to its size. Recent "plus" axioms of proportionality are particularly appealing notions: they are verifiable in polynomial time, and they provide strong representation guarantees without requiring groups of voters to have cohesive preferences. However, their existing formulations are restricted to approval-based preferences. We generalise extended justified representation plus (EJR+), and Core plus (Core+) to general additive utilities. Our approach builds on a payment-based interpretation of proportionality: candidates' costs are shared among their supporters, with the aim of balancing voters' total payments.

2610.18812v1.title: The Geography of (Concurrent) Block Proposing
2610.18812v1.authors: Ciamac C. Moallemi, Mallesh M. Pai, Dan Robinson, Christoph Schlegel
2610.18812v1.ori_summary: The resilience and censorship resistance of a blockchain depend on where the validators and proposers of that blockchain physically operate. We study the economic incentives behind this location choice, both with a single proposer and with multiple concurrent proposers. Formally, we study a game where proposers first choose locations and then compete in a first-price auction for an opportunity whose common value is driven by information from geographically dispersed sources. A single proposer minimizes variance-weighted delay, locating at a weighted median of the sources and co-locating with any dominant one. By contrast, with two proposers, information both observe equally early earns no rent, and each proposer's expected profit is proportional to the standard deviation of the information it receives before its rival. We show that the location game admits the jointly unobserved variance as an ordinal potential, so global solutions of a weighted two-median problem are equilibria. With two sources, one proposer locates at each, however weak one is. With more proposers and at least as many sources, equilibrium locations are distinct under regular bidding. Multiple concurrent proposers thus do more than limit any single proposer's control over inclusion: by rewarding exclusive rather than shared information, they create an economic force toward geographic decentralization.
